hook: Two people see the same car crash. A week later one remembers broken glass on the road and the other does not. There was no broken glass. The only difference: one was asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed" into each other. Memory is not a recording. It can fade, get blocked, and be rewritten.

prereq.q: Which strategy is most likely to reduce forgetting before a test four weeks away?
prereq.why: The spacing effect: distributed practice gives better long-term retention.

prereq.q: Why is recognition usually easier than recall?
options: The options act as retrieval cues
prereq.why: In recognition the options themselves cue the stored memory.

figure.caption: Ebbinghaus's (1885) forgetting curve: fast loss at first, then a slow tail.

chain.cause: Other learning competes with a memory
chain.effect: retrieval is blocked (proactive or retroactive interference)

chain.cause: A memory is retrieved and rebuilt
chain.effect: gaps are filled with expectations (constructive memory)

chain.cause: Misleading information or repeated imagining comes in during rebuilding
chain.effect: confident false memories form (misinformation effect, imagination inflation)

ideas: The forgetting curve: much is lost quickly, then the rest fades slowly. Spacing and retrieval practice flatten it.
Forgetting can be encoding failure (never stored), interference (proactive: old blocks new; retroactive: new blocks old), or retrieval failure (the tip-of-the-tongue state).
Repression is the psychodynamic account of forgetting threatening memories; the evidence for it is weak.
Memory is constructive: the misinformation effect, source amnesia and imagination inflation can create confident false memories.

misconception.wrong: If someone remembers an event vividly and confidently, the memory must be accurate.
misconception.right: Confidence and vividness do not guarantee accuracy. Memories are rebuilt each time they are recalled, and misleading questions or repeated imagining can add details that never happened.

summary: We forget quickly at first and then more slowly (the forgetting curve). Forgetting comes from encoding failure, interference (proactive and retroactive) and retrieval failure; repression is the psychodynamic account, with weak evidence. Because memory is reconstructed, misleading information, forgotten sources and imagination can produce confident false memories.
